planting.note: Plant root cuttings (crowns or side-root 'thongs') a few weeks before last frost into deeply worked soil; this is the main commercial strain grown in the Illinois horseradish belt.

directions: Bohemian (sometimes sold as Common horseradish) is the principal cultivar grown in the major U.S. horseradish-producing districts of southern Illinois, prized for smooth, straight roots and reliable pungency. It is set out from root cuttings rather than seed, with angled planting of the thong encouraging a single tapering root instead of a forked one. Give it a dedicated bed, since any root fragment left behind will resprout and the planting becomes effectively permanent. Roots are dug in autumn or after a hard frost, when cold weather has concentrated the pungent oils that give horseradish its bite.

planting.note: Plant root cuttings a few weeks before last frost in deep, loose soil; this is the other major commercial strain alongside Bohemian/Common horseradish in U.S. production.

directions: Big Top Western is one of the two cultivars (alongside Bohemian/Common) that dominate commercial horseradish acreage in the United States, grown for vigorous root production and good disease tolerance in heavier soils. Like other horseradish strains it is propagated vegetatively from pencil-thick side roots saved from the previous harvest rather than from seed. It spreads aggressively from any left-behind root fragments, so growers typically rotate or contain the planting site. Roots are harvested in fall once cold weather has driven starches toward root growth and intensified the characteristic sharp flavor.

planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring once frost danger has passed; this Australian rainforest conifer wants warmth and is only reliably hardy in mild, frost-free to nearly frost-free climates.

directions: Hoop pine is a tall Australian conifer with distinctively tiered, horizontally whorled branches and a straight trunk marked with characteristic horizontal hoop-like ridges in the bark, from which it takes its common name. Juvenile foliage is soft, narrow, and needle-like while mature upper-crown foliage becomes shorter, denser, and more scale-like, giving older specimens a layered, almost pagoda-like silhouette. It is an important forestry timber species in its native Queensland and New South Wales and is also planted as a large specimen or avenue tree in warm, frost-free landscapes. Give it deep, well-drained soil and full sun, and plenty of room, since it ultimately grows into a massive canopy tree unsuited to small home gardens.
sources: Queensland Government Department of Agriculture and Fisheries

planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring in a frost-free to nearly frost-free climate; it is commonly planted as a street and park tree in coastal California, Hawaii, and Florida.

directions: Cook pine is a narrow, strongly columnar conifer from New Caledonia, with short branches held close to a slender trunk that gives mature trees a distinctive spire-like profile very different from the broader, tiered look of most araucarias. Many mature specimens, especially in Northern Hemisphere plantings, develop a consistent and much-discussed lean toward the equator, a quirk that has made the species a minor botanical curiosity in California and Hawaii. It tolerates coastal wind, salt spray, and lean, well-drained soils once established, which has made it a popular avenue and park tree in mild coastal climates. Give it full sun and good drainage, and avoid colder inland sites where it has little frost tolerance.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

common_name: Aurea Nana Dwarf Golden Oriental Arborvitae

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this old, widely grown dwarf selection is a classic formal-garden and rock-garden conifer.

directions: Aurea Nana is a long-cultivated dwarf form of oriental arborvitae that builds a dense, rounded-to-ovoid bush of upright, flattened sprays, much smaller and slower-growing than the species. New growth emerges bright yellow-gold and gradually mellows toward yellow-green through summer, with some bronzing possible in winter cold. Its compact, globe-like habit needs little to no shearing to stay tidy, making it useful for low formal hedging, foundation plantings, and rock gardens. Full sun brings out the best gold color and keeps growth dense; in shade it fades toward green and becomes looser and more open.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in deep, moist, well-drained, acidic soil; it tends to be hardier and more reliably blue than straight-species seedlings.

directions: Blue China fir is a selected form of China fir with stiff, sharply pointed, glaucous blue-green needles that give the whole tree a cooler, more silvery cast than the green-leaved species. It keeps the same bold, somewhat architectural pyramidal habit and shaggy, reddish-brown peeling bark, and like the species it often resprouts vigorously from the base or stump if damaged. Old lower branches can brown and drop needles over time, which is normal and is best addressed by underplanting rather than fighting it with pruning. Grow in deep, moisture-retentive, acidic soil out of harsh winter wind, where it makes a striking specimen tree with year-round blue-green color.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; protect from harsh winter sun and wind, which can scorch the gold foliage.

directions: Ogon is a golden-needled selection of Japanese umbrella pine, carrying the same thick, glossy, radially whorled 'spokes' of foliage as the species but in bright yellow-gold rather than dark green, especially on new growth. Growth is slow like all umbrella pines, gradually building a dense, narrow pyramidal form that rewards patience with an increasingly striking color accent in the conifer garden. Afternoon shade helps prevent the gold foliage from scorching in hot climates while still keeping enough light exposure for good color development. Plant in rich, acidic, evenly moist but well-drained soil, since this species dislikes both drought and waterlogging at the root.
